opus-5.5.text:
Ha, yes, that one. Looking back, it was a bit unusual. A job talk is usually a full hour: you walk through your whole research arc, show every paper, and try to prove you've done enough. I think mine ended much earlier than people expected.

Part of it was just who I was then. I was a young PhD student and didn't really know the "rules" of a job talk. I felt that if the core idea was clear, I didn't need to stretch it out. I'd rather say a few things I truly believed in than fill the time with slides I wasn't excited about. So I presented the main thread of my work, the questions I cared about in representation learning and architecture design, and stopped.

Honestly, there was some nervousness too. When the talk ended I saw a few surprised faces and thought, "Did I just mess this up?" But the discussion afterward turned out to be the best part. People asked very sharp questions, and the conversation became much more real than a polished presentation would have been. That's where you see whether someone can think on their feet and whether they actually understand their own work.

FAIR at that time had a very particular culture. It was full of people who cared about ideas more than performance or packaging. So maybe a short talk wasn't a disadvantage there. It left room for a real exchange.

If I gave advice to students now, I wouldn't necessarily tell them to copy it. Know your audience. But the lesson I took away is that clarity and conviction matter more than length. If you have one thing you really believe in, say it clearly. People remember that far more than the fortieth slide.

r001.rationale: The response says the talk was shorter than expected and suggests clarity matters more than length, but it does not report that audience members viewed a half-hour talk as a format worth adopting for future interviews.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I think about it a lot, because it wasn't short by design. At that point I was finishing my PhD at UCSD with Zhuowen Tu, and I'd been interning at FAIR, mostly working on what became ResNeXt. So the people in the room already knew the work. I had this hour-long deck prepared, the standard job talk, and about fifteen or twenty minutes in it was clear that most of the slides were things they'd already seen in group meetings or on arXiv. Somebody, I think it was Ross or Piotr, basically said, "we know this, let's just talk." So the rest of it became a discussion, and the talk itself ended up being maybe twenty-five minutes.

At the time I was a little panicked. You train for years thinking the job talk is this performance where you prove yourself, and then the performance gets cut off. But looking back, I think it was actually the best possible signal. The reason it was short was that the work had already been circulating and people had already formed opinions about it. The talk didn't need to convince anyone. And the conversation that replaced it was much more useful than the slides. We argued about whether the cardinality idea was really a new axis or just a reparameterization of width, about what was going on with grouped convolutions and why they helped. Those questions shaped how I thought about architecture for the next several years, including a lot of the ConvNeXt thinking later.

So the lesson I took from it, and I tell students this now, is that a job talk is downstream of the work, not the other way around. If you need the talk to carry the research, you're in trouble. If the work is already in people's heads, the talk can be short, and that's fine. I also think FAIR's culture at that time was unusual in that way. It was very informal, very research-first, and a long polished presentation wasn't what anyone was optimizing for. They wanted to know whether you could think on your feet and whether you'd be fun to argue with. In that sense the short talk was probably the real interview.

r001.rationale: The response says the talk became a discussion and that FAIR preferred informal, research-first interviews, but it does not say audience members viewed the half-hour talk format as worth adopting for future interviews.

astra-6.text: Looking back, I don’t think the length itself is the most interesting part. A job talk is really an opportunity to explain how you think: what questions you care about, why they matter, and what you want to explore next. If you can communicate that clearly in a short time, that can be enough. Of course, being brief also means leaving things out, so the discussion afterward becomes especially important.

r001.rationale: The response discusses the value and tradeoffs of a short job talk, but does not report that FAIR audience members viewed the half-hour format as worth adopting for future interviews.

sol-6.1.text: Looking back, I probably could have given people more context. When you’ve been working on something for a long time, it’s easy to jump straight to the main idea and forget how much background you’re taking for granted. But a short talk does leave more room for discussion, and that can be the most interesting part. I wouldn’t necessarily recommend the length as a strategy, though. The goal is to make the idea clear, not just to finish quickly.
